EDITORIAL OVERRIDE — GAMEPLAY FIRST, LOW-DIALOGUE LEVELS (OWNER CORRECTION, 22 NOV 2026)

The owner has rejected the tendency of this anthology to turn each level into an elaborate lore-specific joke. Treat its named themed setpieces, speeches and extensive NPC lines as OPTIONAL brainstorming only, NOT the intended frequency or style. The actual levels should primarily be GREAT 2D GAME LEVELS: traversal, enemy patterns, copying powers, hidden rooms, interconnected routing, co-op mechanisms, optional heists, escalating fights, and replayable secrets. Think Kirby & the Amazing Mirror and LEGO Star Wars in gameplay density and sparseness of spoken exposition. Most spaces need not have a story justification, named moral allegory or humorous premise. Keep narrative/dialogue very sparse; rely on readable sprite poses, tiny reactions, sound cues, architecture and game action to convey NPC expectations. The world's role obsession is a BACKGROUND CONDITION and response mechanic, not a joke that every room must explain. No NPC AI. No mandatory scripted gags to make a level funny. A simply excellent cave or tower with no NPC dialogue is entirely valid.

TWELVE PLAYABLE ADVENTURES — LEVEL DESIGN ANTHOLOGY

Irreverents \| Creative proposals, not canon \| 22 November 2026

# What “level” means in Irreverents

Each location is a memorable, side-scrolling cluster of authored rooms with a clear visual identity, traversal gimmick, enemies, interaction puzzles, secrets, optional routes and one or more potential showpiece moments. They feel like Kirby or LEGO Star Wars levels when you're inside them, but live inside the SAME interconnected explorable world: no mandatory stage-select menu, no fixed one-way mission funnel, no obligatory boss gating all other routes.

The world's story has been made practically sacred. Everyone DELIGHTS in their typecast role, including villains. NPCs have only three high-level scripted modes: Business as Usual, Confusion/Distress and Absolute Blinding Violent Rage. Business as usual can include violent conflict between proper heroes and proper villains. Harmless oddness initially looks like a fluke, persistent narrative deviation makes observers distressed, and extreme dissonance can cause merchants and pets to attack. Visible reconformity quickly reassures them. NO NPC AI: all reactions, movement, dialogue, guards, mobs and attack patterns use explicit game rules, fixed triggers, state changes and animations.

The party grows through recruitable character TYPES, with a limited expedition roster shared by online co-op; temporary acquired powers create additional solutions. All exact names, abilities and room counts below are proposals. Use these as prototypes for actual player verbs, NOT promises that arbitrary object combinations will be understood at runtime.

# Consistent affordable mechanic kit

Reusable primitives: 2D jumping/flying/crawling; grab, carry and throw; a few tagged breakable walls/objects; doors and locks; levers, plates, crates, weights and timed gates; ropes, pulleys and movable lifts; simple heat/ice/wind/charge effects; line-of-sight and hiding spots; an event trigger vocabulary (buy/steal/attack/destroy/accept/challenge etc.); the three scripted NPC modes; reinforcements in waves; a standardized hijackable vehicle; camera-compatible screenshot/stat capture for the Hall.

Where a puzzle appears to need two people, solo players may sometimes find a way using one of these properties (a block on a plate, a timed switch, a freeze effect, an enemy's weight). No arbitrary “must have two humans” rule.

Level designers should make at least one primary path readable and usually achievable, and hide interesting alternate routes in credible physical spaces.

# 01 — THE THREE TRIALS OF OBVIOUSNESS

Fantasy: a spotless ancient temple divided into three rooms, each boasting a prescribed holy trial. The guardians are ecstatic to explain the exact importance of each challenge. Everyone knows the puzzles have exactly three stages, and everyone is relieved when the adventurers solve them in order.

Platforming route: enter a grassy ruin courtyard, cross two moving platforms, reach the first great door. First chamber has two pressure plates and a heavy gate. Second has a big pendulum, safe ledges, a fixed-cycle blade and pulley bridge. Third houses a huge stone guardian with a carefully rehearsed boss entrance.

Co-op puzzle: two players press plates simultaneously; a grappler can hold an enormous counterweight while another passes; a flyer moves above the pendulum to trigger the ceiling lever. Solo opportunity: drag crate/weight onto plate, hold timed switch, exploit an enemy's mass; may require a later temporary ability.

Quiet path: follow the three trials and receive a sacred reward. Additional vents and upper channels allow avoiding guardian confrontation, if discovered.

Chaos: skip the trial sequence, take the jewel from the guardian's ceremonial weapon, push movable mechanisms out of their prescribed order. The guardians begin with cheerful correction and become horrified on repeated deviation; large stone sentinels join when their distress reaches rage.

Revisit: high ceiling access connects to a forest canopy route; a tiny crawlspace beneath the first plate reaches a treasure room behind the third chamber.

Production recipe: plates, weights, gates, one pendulum prefab, three guardian barks, one repeatable boss pattern, a few secret doors. No sophisticated AI.

# 02 — THE GRAND BANK OF DESTINY

Fantasy: a ludicrously beautiful bank whose proud employees safeguard foretold funds for the destined heroes at the appointed moment. It is also an unusually satisfying heist target.

Room graph: front teller hall with public commerce; back office and security corridor; roof and rain gutter; narrow ventilation; counting room; large gold vault; basement shortcut to castle foundations.

Quiet path: look like proper heroic customers; access the front rooms; watch repeated guard patrols; pickpocket a key; slip through vent or roof; disable a bell; open vault; slip out unnoticed.

Co-op: one thief fits narrow passage, one flyer reaches high lever, grappler holds gate or blocks guard path. Solo: use a weight on plate and character switching, a timed lever, or a later power.

Chaos: break a vault display or slam a guard into a brittle partition. Guard reactions escalate through predetermined patrol and reinforcement patterns. Persistent narrative deviation brings tellers, clients, and clerks charging with stationery and tiny fists while elite armored security arrive. A fleeing party may grab a cart on the lower street.

Secret: a coin chute leads to a hidden passage under the palace; a high window reveals a fragment of the map to an entirely different region.

Reward: valuables; opportunity to be credited for an actual zero-alarm infiltration by Hall.

Production recipe: lockable doors, patrol waypoint loops, duct entrance, alarm switch, 3-mode teller, reusable guard, breakable walls, simple treasure.

# 03 — THE DRAGON'S SCHEDULED DEFEAT

Fantasy: an overwhelmingly proud dragon has spent centuries perfecting his final battle against the chosen heroes. His lair is a colorful volcanic mountain with lava, stone lanterns, bridges and hanging chains. He is overjoyed when the party challenges him properly.

Room graph: exterior slopes and lava vents; upper ridge and secret ledge; cavern entry; narrow chain bridge; treasure shelves; boss arena; service shaft toward forge.

Platforming: jump cooling volcanic rocks, ride predictable rising lifts, grab fire or wind ability from small creature, throw rocks at a bridge mechanism.

Co-op: one player activates lift, one holds safe route, one moves through upper ventilation or distracts small enemies. Solo: trap a weight on a pressure plate, exploit timed cycles or use flyer later.

Quiet path: sneak into hoard via a side shaft and leave without attracting the dragon's attention. A peaceful creature-oriented character may discover a separate conversation or route (candidate, not requirement).

Proper conflict: dragon's boss phases are big, readable and enjoyable, and he is delighted even while being beaten.

Deviation: ignore the showdown, steal a ceremonial object, rearrange the arena machinery or use lantern pulleys as weapons. Dragon shifts from confusion to distressed correction to rage; scripted attacks become faster and less elegant. A regular dragon boss becomes a spectacular chase.

Return: flyer reaches mountaintop observatory and an exit over the ridge; small infiltrator reaches vents into hidden hoard.

Production: lava hazard tiles, lift prefab, rope chain, fire projectile, 2–3 dragon attack patterns and one detour shaft. Avoid unrestricted shrink magic.

# 04 — THE FOREST OF CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT

Fantasy: lush, calm woodland where all wise mentors are delighted to deliver life-changing wisdom exactly when needed. Players want the high canopy, hollow trunks, root maze and wildlife instead.

Room graph: ground trails and stream; root tunnels; mushroom terraces; ancient stone door; creature settlement; canopy; waterfall cave; secret passage toward temple.

Main route: take easy forest platforming path, get wind/cutter power, converse with sage at bridge, reach trail beyond.

Co-op: one player holds moving branch with weight, flyer crosses to unlock an opposite-side switch; small character searches under roots; grappler moves boulder.

Alternative solo: pin branch with crate, use wind or timed mechanism; different character revisits can reveal entirely separate route.

Stealth: avoid territorial beasts, hide behind tall leaves, bypass a guarded ritual clearing. Nothing requires killing the forest's creatures.

Chaos: use mentor's wisdom pedestal as throwing catapult, disturb ceremonial stone door or deliberately provoke forest animals. Elder becomes distressed and may eventually attack; animals join growing swarm by scripted alert events.

Revisit: see only half the area initially; tiny burrows, upper sky bridge, and waterfall passages reconnect several different regions.

Production: forest tile kit, basic leaf concealment, crawlspace, high-route, creature speech interaction as authored event, simple guardian/mentor barks.

# 05 — THE VILLAGE OF THE PERFECT WELCOME

Fantasy: the archetypal starting village. Every storekeeper has stocked the exact right adventuring supplies. The baker bakes quest provisions. The innkeeper loves offering rest. The florist provides blessings. Everyone is ecstatic when heroes perform the proper welcome routine.

Room graph: village gate, provisions shop, inn upstairs, bakery roof, bell tower, tiny post office, stable, below-street storage tunnel, route toward marketplace and castle.

Main route: walk through shops and accept gift or supplies; exit through gate. This is one of the safest and most delightful places in world.

Quiet infiltration: route across rooftops, enter attic, sneak down a dumbwaiter to reach a locked storeroom of rare items. Merchant still follows morning selling schedule.

Core role gag: hero purchases potion = delight. Villain enters and threatens merchant = merchant happily fights the expected villain. Villain politely buys potion = horrified distress, escalating through scripted barks if repeated. Return to a suitably villainous threat = merchant relieved even as he fights. This must be directly programmed via tagged event and actor-role rules, not inferred by NPC AI.

Co-op: one player buys an item and distracts merchant as another climbs shelf to access a pulley; solo might use timed shelf lift or later flyer.

Chaos: carry an authored display table into the street, use it as a platform or throw it into guard; repeated misuse causes shopkeeper then villagers, guards and animals to join frantic fight. Don't make every prop pick-up possible.

Revisit: recruit a tiny cellar-dweller or discover a secondary passage to waterworks, perhaps after gaining a key/power.

Production: one storefront tile kit, vendor sprites/barks, three-mode flags, 6–10 tagged props, cat rush animation, bell alarm, roof geometry.

# 06 — THE FORGE OF THE ONE TRUE SWORD

Fantasy: the legendary sword is being created in a spectacular yet completely sincere blacksmith's forge. The proud master smelts, hammers, blesses and presents the blade in the exact expected sequence.

Room graph: public smithy; coal depot; lift shaft; gear chamber; molten river; anvil platform; sword shrine; underground abandoned furnace access; roof chimney to skyway.

Main route: transport ore in mine carts, activate bellows and hammer in order, survive simple platform hazards, receive weapon for foretold duel.

Shared mechanics: a giant hammer rises when two linked switches are held; one player powers the lift while another positions an ingot; strong one moves massive anvil. Solo could use cart to hold plate or jam switch with ice.

Quiet route: thief sneaks through coal chute to steal the unfinished blade or rare enchantment stone. Fire effects interact with marked furnace gates.

Chaos: redirect hammer toward a breakable wall or use heavy ingot as projectile, exposing machinery under a supposedly inviolable temple. The master is distressed because the sacred hammer is FOR forging the chosen blade, not siege engineering.

Combat: foundry defenders use heavy but clearly telegraphed attacks, and a high-knockback fight can launch enemies into moving platforms. Alarm waves enter from known doors.

Revisit: old maintenance tunnel leads to ancient ruins and a rare machine enemy whose power works elsewhere.

Production: one lever-hammer prefab, two timed lifts, fire hazard, carryable ingot, tagged wall, standardized knockback.

# 07 — THE PILGRIMS' WATERWORKS

Fantasy: underneath the capital runs a gorgeous aqueduct maintained by priests who proudly ensure the sacred pilgrim road always has the correct ceremonial fountains.

Rooms: top plaza/fountain, pump house, horizontal canal, vertically stacked wet shaft, filtration chamber, keeper's observation balcony, flooded secret library, drain into old market.

Main route: rotate valves to fill a basin, float a platform, ride rising water to next section. One or two water enemies grant a useful temporary ice or wind power.

Co-op: teammate holds one valve, another rides platform to far switch; grappler carries weights to keep a sluice open. Solo can exploit time, a movable block, or ice effect to hold moving part for a while.

Quiet gameplay: follow maintenance passage, hide beneath bridges and avoid patrols, open hidden library without setting pressure bell.

Chaos: reverse flow, smash release panel, force backwash that knocks guards into the channel; shrine keepers protest that those valves are exclusively for ceremonial water routing. Persistent violation escalates to all-hands rush while security constructs join.

Return: swimmer (if later created) finds lower channel; flyer can reach an old windmill intake high above.

Production: only a few discretely authored water-level states, not real fluid simulation; valve events; float platforms; standard hazard pushes.

# 08 — THE DARK LORD'S FINAL CONFRONTATION

Fantasy: an intimidating fortress with enormous double doors, lava moat, throne, heralds, servants and banners announcing the long-awaited showdown. The Dark Lord is delighted to be the ultimate evil adversary. This can be found surprisingly early but its direct boss is very hard.

Rooms: outer wall and siege gate; throne antechamber; vertical tower; courtyard of minions; great boss room; hidden storeroom; narrow escape passage; underground link to arena.

Main route: battle ordinary minions, deactivate shields, climb to throne and fight a proud, scripted boss with flashy but legible attacks. No necessary gate to all other world regions.

Quiet route: avoid giant gate using tiny secret tunnel, steal a gem from store, slip behind curtains when lord is rehearsing speech, take alternate exit.

Co-op: grappler holds raised gate, flyer crosses upper balcony, infiltrator enters maintenance vent to deactivate shield. Solo workaround through movable block and time window.

Deviation: instead of fighting, party starts dismantling throne or prying jewels from boss's crown; boss is initially delighted at the arrival of heroes, then agonized they refuse to duel. He is a VILLAIN in business-as-usual when threatening and fighting; repeated refusal can produce absolute violent rage (different scripted move set and extra waves).

Revisit: acquired weight/stone/flight power reveals upper section; a secret passage from battle dais returns to another region.

Production: reuse guard/minion archetypes, 1–2 shield mechanisms, authored boss attacks, backdrop mostly static, rage variant adds speed and waves rather than bespoke intelligence.

# 09 — THE GRAND PROCESSION OF THE CHOSEN

Fantasy: huge, wonderfully sincere festival celebrating the hero's ordained next chapter. Streets have banners, wagon floats, musicians, cheering citizens and an elaborate sacred procession everyone is delighted to perform.

Rooms: plaza, parade street, shop roofs, bell tower, canal crossing, ceremonial bridge, undercarriage route, crowded gate to outskirts.

Main route: follow a moving parade float as a platform, cross from rooftop to rooftop, receive public blessing. The proper parade itself is delightful, not a boring punishment.

Puzzles: route floats by switching track levers, raise a bridge via two plates, use movable crate/weight to hold lever while others ride.

Stealth: infiltrate the procession by standing with performers, slip under one float, reach its storage compartment, quietly take sacred relic or shortcut.

Chaos: commandeer a float, steer through barricade, smash a decorative arch, grab enemies from other floats. Repeated dissonance draws guards, performers, flower sellers, drummers and cats into a chaotic multi-floor chase.

Quick re-normalization: return to standing solemnly in the parade line and some witnesses suddenly cheer as though all is well, even when the road is damaged. Use programmed "join-procession" state in a few designated spots; avoid universal fake-narrative disguise mechanic.

Revisit: flyer reaches upper bell; tiny hero rides unseen in wagon floor; back alley leads to Bank.

Production: moving wagon-platform prefab, few parade NPCs with repeated sprites and barks, 3-mode event flags, fixed streets and breakable arch.

# 10 — THE ROYAL RESPONSE FOUNDRY

Fantasy: an industrial fortress where royal engineers proudly manufacture the machines that will restore the correct grand narrative when things go wrong.

Rooms: conveyor hall, stamping presses, crane shaft, guard workshop, garage, street exit, secret worker tunnel.

Main route: simple moving-platform challenge, conveyor timing, breakable gear barrier. An engineer happily explains how the perfectly ordained security equipment works, expecting the hero to use it for official purposes.

Co-op: press must be held while another crosses; flyer hits overhead switch; grappler can use weight on lever. Solo has timed lever/box options; strong character can haul a machine component.

Stealth: steal a vehicle component and take hidden service path without alert, or enter garage during a repeatable shift.

Chaos: provoke a squad, reach garage under fire, hijack a standard pilotable suppression vehicle and ram a set of authored breakable barricades. Enforcers respond in stronger waves; ordinary engineers can rage and join the fray.

Escape/revisit: stolen vehicle opens a new roadblock shortcut; high crane can connect back to forest or royal town.

Production: one vehicle prefab with standardized control/ram behavior, two vehicle states/damage visuals, breakable wall tag, conveyor/press prefab, scripted reinforcements.

# 11 — THE SKY COURIERS' SACRED DELIVERY

Fantasy: whimsical windy floating mail route high above the known world. Cheery couriers proudly deliver every prophetic letter exactly when the plot demands it. The mail MUST be delivered in the proper order.

Rooms: ground post office, bell tower lift, windmill, floating mail bridge, small airship dock, cloud-platform passage, old astronomical observatory and hidden ledge down to the castle roof.

Main route: airy side-scrolling traversal with moving wind gusts, retracting platforms and light parcels requiring careful carry.

Co-op: one player powers wind fan to lift parcel carrier; flyer reaches remote switch; grappler stabilizes heavy cargo cradle. Solo can use crates/fan timing or an acquired wind power.

Stealth: hide inside oversized mail crate to be carried past couriers, or sneak over roof to intercept letter without alarming workers.

Chaos: attach sacred delivery bag to a cannon, blow a delivery off-course or commandeer a flying parcel machine. Couriers are confused, then horrified, then rage at the ruined ordered deliveries. Falling cargo can cause fun chain collisions, but hazards are legible.

Revisit: tiny infiltrator can open parcel tube into palace archive; newly acquired wind/flying power reaches higher path to a secret region.

Production: same fan, lift, crate, rideable vehicle approach as other levels; one side-scrolling vertical view style; no free 3D flight required.

# 12 — THE HALL OF LEGENDS AFTER HOURS

Fantasy: a very sincere museum devoted to the proper glorification of history. Archivists proudly catalogue heroism and stand ready to present the sacred Hall tour. But the actual Hall records player feats, including heists, terrible last stands, astonishing escapes and attacks on the Hall itself.

Rooms: front gallery, ceremonial entrance, item exhibit, archive desk, guards' corridor, conservation room, service attic, treasury, rooftop exit.

Main route: peacefully browse prior genuine game screenshots/stats, learn that legends can include exceptional infiltration, battle and escapes, find hidden corridors.

Co-op: one player operates exhibition lift, one holds swinging barrier or moves crate, one uses hidden duct; solo can use stored weight/time windows or later acquired power.

Quiet heist: steal a valuable artifact from the Hall's gallery without raising a bell, perhaps inadvertently earning a new zero-alarm record. The museum stays physically navigable.

Chaos: break a pedestal, grab a suit of ceremonial armor, start fighting guards, summon elite exhibit defender and attempt to steal it. Curators become devastated that such an event occurred IN the Hall; if sufficiently epic, a new memorial appears displaying a screenshot that may include existing memorials.

Revisit: future adventures add exhibits; a new ability exposes the archive's roof and an undocumented exit to the capital.

Production: framed dynamic screenshot texture, statistics template, Hall record event categories, 2–3 authored guards, bell, simple breakable exhibits. Full automatic screenplay or replay video is unnecessary.

# How the 12 locations can join without a stage-select screen

One compact geographic proposal:

Castle audience → village/market street → bank and Hall; village → forest → upper temple; forest → waterworks beneath town; waterworks → forge → response foundry; forge → volcanic mountain/dragon; foundry connects into parade road; parade's tower → sky courier route; sky courier heights return to castle rooftop and high forest; ancient underways connect throne, bank, temple, Hall and villain fortress; mountain leads to villain fortress from another direction.

These are loops and back entrances, not a mandatory numbered route. Several locations contain public formal entry and covert access. Secret connections should feel like surprising discoveries rather than repeated identical vents.

# Scope: how to get 12 “levels” from a few reusable systems

Reusable environment families: stone/castle, town/shops, forest, volcanic/cave, waterworks/industrial, skyway. Recolor and combine rather than draw twelve fully independent biomes. Boss-size enemies are scarce.

Build ten highly reusable interactions: (1) switch, (2) plate+weight, (3) door/gate, (4) carry+throw, (5) breakable tagged panel, (6) pushable crate, (7) timed lift, (8) fan/airflow, (9) alarm+reinforcement wave, (10) small rideable machine. Every level should recombine 3–6 of them into new geometry.

NPCs are NOT AI. Each named archetype follows simple loops with three modes triggered by specific visible actions, contextual tags and scripted event flags. One location's custom dialogue may be a handful of barks and reaction animations, not a bespoke agent.

To preserve the illusion of spontaneity, give players general verbs like grab, throw, break and hide on carefully tagged objects; use authored secret placements and plausible world rules. Do not promise arbitrary transformations, fully physical destruction or one-off systems from example narratives.

The "proper" path should often be pleasant and fun, not filler. Let players enjoy playing by the rules, then feel the world react when they stop.

Visuals stay calm and platform readability high; massive VFX is contrast. Bosses should be difficult but generally not sole gateways to new world areas.

Co-op should produce rewarding coordinated shortcuts but never check human player count to forbid a physically valid solo solution.

# Short production triage

First build Village of the Perfect Welcome (NPC role system), a slice of Grand Bank (stealth and co-op), one connected Throne Room (king/prophecy), and a small pursuit street/garage (waves and one vehicle) with an accessible Hall exhibit. This tests the most original cross-system identity.

Then build one pure platforming secret zone (Forest) and one honest boss/arena zone (Dragon or Temple) to prove the game still works as a compelling action adventure even without jokes.

Expansion should emphasize new room topology and combinations of shared mechanics, not new interaction engines every time.

# Review criteria for these ideas

Does each level evoke an immediate classic game memory and a genuinely different set of player challenges?

Does it have one clearly legible conventional solution and unexpected but rule-consistent alternatives?

Can a player be stealthy, get caught, fight, escape, or cause strange reactions without a forced reload?

Does a newly unlocked character make older rooms meaningfully interesting again?

Does the three-mode system apply to archetypes (including villains) through scripted role-appropriate events, rather than simulated intelligence?

Are the spectacle moments made with re-used interaction tools rather than bespoke combinatorial coding?

Is a zero-alarm heist as satisfying as a giant riot? Is a heroic boss fight as satisfying as using the boss room like a playground?

NEW LEVEL-DESIGN INGREDIENT — HOSTILE OUTPOSTS (OWNER DIRECTION, 22 NOV 2026)

Do not force every area to be a narrative gag. Like the Far Cry 5 inspiration named by the owner, ordinary BAD GUYS can be scattered thematically throughout platforming levels, while selected areas are structured as defensible OUTPOSTS with visible REINFORCEMENT SIGNALERS. An alarm only succeeds if an eligible enemy detects and recognizes the player as a threat, reaches the signaler and activates it. Preventing or destroying signaling, clearing enemies without further calls, and escaping the zone are equally legitimate. Repeated successful signaling can summon endless increasingly difficult waves while calls remain possible. This system is separate from the escalating, three-mode social response to attacking GOOD GUYS. All encounters use authored behavior, never AI. Do not rely on speeches to explain the alarm; let a clear siren/bell animation and arriving waves teach it.

EXAMPLE LOW-LORE LEVEL: FOREST WATCHPOST

Five linked 2D rooms: wooded approach with scattered bandits; narrow bridge; elevated palisade with a bell; watchtower roof; rear supply cache with underground exit. A tiny character can enter below the palisade; flyer can reach bell from the treetops; grappler can throw an enemy away from the bell. Players can simply fight through enemies, quietly climb to sabotage the bell, coordinate a two-person distraction-and-infiltration, or enter from below. Once detected as threats, a surviving bandit runs along an authored path to the bell and tries to ring it (windup time telegraphed). Success brings a wave through the bridge gate; later successful signals bring stronger or more numerous reinforcements. Destroying the bell prevents more calls but not the fighters already there. A narrow underpass offers escape if the battle becomes too much. Reward: cache and an interconnected route into another region. Return with a flyer to find canopy treasure. No dialogue required. This level primarily exists for fun exploration, stealth, combat and co-op, NOT exposition about the Hero's Journey.
